analysis.one_liner: Adds offshore oil and gas lease sales without reapproval, and waives environmental review for Gulf of Mexico sales.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have let the government add new offshore drilling lease sales without reworking its five-year leasing plan — and skip environmental review for Gulf of Mexico sales — died in the Senate Energy Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, the federal government follows an approved five-year schedule for selling offshore oil and gas drilling rights, and adding sales to that schedule requires going back through an approval process. This bill would let officials add extra lease sales whenever they want, without that reapproval. It also declares that lease sales in the Gulf of Mexico do not count as a "major federal action" under the National Environmental Policy Act, the law that requires environmental impact reviews, so Gulf lease sales could go forward without one.
analysis.who_benefits: Offshore oil and gas companies gain the most: more lease sales mean more access to public waters for drilling, and the Gulf exemption removes a layer of environmental review that can delay sales and create legal openings for opponents. Gulf Coast states that collect drilling revenue shares would also gain.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act so the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management can add lease sales to an approved five-year leasing program without the reapproval that normally applies to significant changes [S2] [S3].

It declares that Gulf of Mexico lease sales are not a "major federal action" under the National Environmental Policy Act, exempting them from the environmental impact statements that other offshore lease sales would still require [S3].
The added sales would still be subject to the general considerations the law requires for a leasing program, and the Secretary retains discretion over whether and when to hold them [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The costs fall on the public lands and waters themselves and on the people who use them: coastal communities, fishing and tourism businesses, and taxpayers who bear the environmental and spill risks of expanded drilling in the Gulf, with the environmental review process — the public's main chance to formally weigh in on a lease sale — bypassed for that region.

drawbacks.text: Waiving NEPA review for Gulf of Mexico lease sales removes the formal environmental impact analysis and public comment process that applies to lease sales elsewhere, including scrutiny of spill risks — a notable tradeoff for the region that produced the Deepwater Horizon disaster [S3].

Allowing lease sales to be added without reapproval of the five-year program weakens a structured planning process that lets communities, states, and conservation interests weigh in on where and when drilling expands [S2] [S3].

Supporters' strongest objection is that the existing approval process is slow and unpredictable, delaying lease sales that Gulf Coast economies and domestic energy production depend on; the bill keeps Secretary discretion and statutory leasing considerations, so it does not force sales to occur.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is faster, more flexible access to offshore drilling rights for energy producers and added revenue for Gulf states. The cost is concentrated on the Gulf itself: the region targeted for the exemption is the one whose lease sales would lose the environmental review process entirely, and the planning reapproval that gave coastal states and the public a formal say would become optional. The bill was designed to lower barriers for industry more than to add any new protection for the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it, so the bill died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Cassidy introduced the bill on March 15, 2017, with three Republican cosponsors: Sens. Tillis, Kennedy, and Cochran [S1] [S3] [S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources on the day it was introduced [S5] [S1].
That referral was the only action ever taken; there were no hearings, no committee vote, and no floor action recorded for the rest of the 115th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coastal communities, Gulf fishing and tourism interests, and conservation advocates came out ahead, since the Gulf NEPA exemption and the shortcut around leasing-program reapproval never became law. The offshore drilling industry lost a chance at expanded lease access it would have gained.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, but the bill never reached a vote, so no roll calls exist to show how support or opposition actually split.

industries.note: The bill would give drillers more lease sales in public waters and remove environmental review for Gulf sales, lowering their costs and legal risk while leaving spill and pollution risks with the public. It was drafted for their benefit and died before delivering it.

industries.industry: Gulf Coast fishing and tourism businesses
industries.note: Expanded drilling without environmental review raises spill and habitat risks for the fisheries and beaches these businesses depend on. They had nothing to gain from the bill and would have borne its environmental cost.

States like Louisiana share revenue from offshore drilling and would gain from more lease sales, but the same activity exposes their coastlines to spill risk. Sponsors from these states backed the bill; the environmental tradeoff fell on the same states.
